flashcards.front: "The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead." Why?
flashcards.back: Because the Spirit is eternal. Arjuna grieves for those not worthy of grief while speaking words of wisdom.

flashcards.front: Childhood, youth, old age, and then?
flashcards.back: Just as the soul passes through these bodies in one life, it acquires a new body after death. The wise are not deluded by this.

flashcards.front: Who slays, and who is slain?
flashcards.back: Neither. One who thinks the Spirit slays or is slain is ignorant: the Spirit neither slays nor is slain.
As a person puts on new clothes after discarding old ones, the soul takes new bodies after casting off the old.

flashcards.front: Unmanifest before birth and after death
flashcards.back: Beings are visible only between birth and death. What is there to grieve about?

flashcards.front: Pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat
flashcards.back: Treat them alike and do your duty; done this way, duty brings no sin.
You control your duty only, never its results. Results should not be your only motive, and you should never be inactive.
Doing your best with your mind on the Lord, free of worry and attachment to results, calm in success and failure. That calmness is Karma-yoga.
Arjuna thought avoiding battle was compassion. Krishna shows that compassion includes doing what is right, even when painful.

flashcards.front: Why can the soul's eternity give courage?
flashcards.back: If death is not the end, danger loses its hold, and one can do what is right even when afraid.
Arjuna could fight from anger or fear, or with understanding of the soul and his duty. The inner understanding changes the act.
Unperturbed by sorrow, free of craving, and free from attachment, fear and anger.

flashcards.front: From thinking of objects to anger (2.62)
flashcards.back: Thinking of sense objects breeds attachment; attachment breeds desire; unfulfilled desire becomes anger.
A mind run by roving senses steals away the intellect, as a storm carries a boat away from the spiritual shore.
Peace comes when desires enter the mind without disturbing it, as rivers enter the full ocean. One who craves objects is never peaceful.

quiz.text: According to 2.47, what do we have control over?
quiz.why: We control our duty, never its fruits, and should never be inactive.

quiz.text: Why do the wise not grieve for the living or the dead?
quiz.why: 2.11 and what follows: the soul never dies, so grief for it is misplaced.

quiz.text: Which image does 2.22 use for rebirth?

options.A: A lamp in a windless place

quiz.why: The soul casts off old bodies and takes new ones, as we change clothes.

options.B: Calmness of mind in success and failure

quiz.why: Doing your best, unattached to results, calm in both outcomes: that calm is Karma-yoga.

quiz.text: Arjuna thought avoiding the battle was compassion. Krishna says:

options.B: True compassion includes doing what is right

quiz.why: Running from duty is not kindness; compassion and duty go together.

quiz.text: In 2.62, what does unfulfilled desire become?
quiz.why: Thinking of objects breeds attachment, then desire, and unfulfilled desire becomes anger.

quiz.text: "Spirit neither slays nor is slain" corrects which assumption?
quiz.why: Arjuna assumed killing bodies meant killing souls; wisdom questions that.

quiz.text: What makes the same outer action wise or ignorant?
quiz.why: Fighting from anger or fear differs completely from fighting with knowledge of the soul and duty.
Peace is like the full ocean receiving rivers; craving objects destroys it.

quiz.text: Why does knowing the soul is eternal let one act with courage?
quiz.why: Physical danger loses its power when death is not the end.
